title: Desert Survival - Heat, Water, Night Travel, and Signaling
summary: How to stay alive when stranded or lost in hot desert country: save sweat instead of rationing water, stay with your vehicle, move only in cool hours, and make yourself easy to find.

steps.title: Stop, get in shade, and take stock
steps.body: The desert kills by heat and water loss, usually within one or two days in summer. The moment you realize you are stranded or lost, stop moving in the sun. Get into shade - under a vehicle awning, a tarp, a rock overhang, or a shade shelter (see shelter-009). Then count your resources: total water in gallons or liters, food, clothing, phone battery, signaling gear, and how many people you have. Tell everyone the plan out loud. Panic makes people walk off into the heat, which is one of the most common ways desert emergencies turn deadly. Desert summer air often tops 100 F (38 C) and can exceed 120 F (49 C) in places like Death Valley, and the ground can be far hotter.

steps.title: Stay with the vehicle
steps.body: If you broke down or got stuck, stay with your car unless you are certain help is a short, cool walk away on a known road. Park rangers in hot desert parks give the same advice: a vehicle is far easier for searchers to see than a person, it holds your supplies, and it gives shade. Do not sit inside a closed car in the sun - it turns into an oven. Sit in shade beside it, open the doors and windows for airflow, or rig a tarp from the roof. Raise the hood, which signals trouble to passersby and aircraft. If you must stay inside during peak heat, keep windows open and stay out of direct sun.

steps.title: Drink your water - ration sweat, not water
steps.body: Drink when you are thirsty and keep drinking; water does more good inside you than in the bottle. Rationing water while you sweat it out speeds up heat illness. Instead, cut sweat loss: rest in shade from late morning to late afternoon, keep your clothes on (loose, light-colored, long sleeves and a wide-brimmed hat), keep your mouth closed, and do not talk or work more than needed. Desert parks advise carrying at least 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day, and 2 gallons (7.6 L) for hiking in heat, plus an emergency reserve. Do not drink alcohol. Eat only if you have water, since digesting food uses water. If you have salty snacks, eat some with water during long heat exposure. For finding more water, see water-012.

steps.title: Watch for heat illness in everyone
steps.body: Check each other every hour. Dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps, heavy sweating, or weakness mean heat exhaustion is starting: move that person to the coolest shade, have them drink, wet their clothing, and fan them. Confusion, strange behavior, collapse, or a hot body with altered thinking is heat stroke, a life-threatening emergency that needs rapid cooling and evacuation - see the heat illness guides in the Medical category. Children, older adults, and people on heart or blood pressure medicines get into trouble faster. Do not let anyone go off alone to 'look for help' while showing heat symptoms.

steps.title: If you must move, move at night or at dawn
steps.body: Walking is a last resort - for example, nobody knows where you are and you know exactly where the nearest road or water is. If you go, travel in the cool hours: from dusk through the night and into early morning, then shelter in shade by mid-morning. Carry all your water, a light, a whistle, and warm layers, because desert nights can drop 30-40 F (17-22 C) and feel cold. Follow roads, tracks, or power lines rather than heading cross-country. Leave a note on the vehicle with your names, direction, time you left, and your plan, and mark your route with arrows of rocks. Watch your footing for holes, cactus, and snakes; use a light at night.

steps.title: Make yourself easy to find
steps.body: Try 911 first; even a weak signal may get a text through, and many newer phones can send emergency texts by satellite where there is no cell service. Turn off apps to save battery and check for signal from high ground every hour or so. In daylight, flash a signal mirror (or any shiny object) at aircraft and distant vehicles (see comms-001). Lay out bright items, a tarp, or rocks in a big X or SOS shape on open ground. Use three whistle blasts, a pause, then repeat. At night, flash a light in the SOS pattern sparingly. A smoky signal fire is visible for miles, but only light it if fire danger allows and you can control it (see comms-003).

steps.title: Respect desert storms and cold
steps.body: Deserts also flood. Summer monsoon storms can send flash floods down dry washes from storms miles away, even under blue sky overhead - never camp or park in a wash, and climb to high ground if you hear a roar or see muddy water (see env-013). Lightning is common with these storms (see env-012). In winter, desert nights can bring frost and even snow, so a stranded person needs warm layers and insulation from the ground. Plan for both extremes before you go: tell someone your route and return time, carry extra water, a spare tire and inflator, and know that tow help may be hours away.

warnings: Never leave a person or pet inside a closed vehicle in desert heat - temperatures inside climb to deadly levels within minutes.
Walking away from a vehicle in daytime heat is a leading cause of desert deaths - stay put unless you have a solid reason and a plan.
Rationing water while working hard or sweating speeds up heat stroke. Drink, and reduce sweat instead.
Do not drink radiator fluid, urine, or alcohol as water substitutes.
Dry washes can flash flood with no rain where you are standing.
proTips: Before any desert drive, leave your route, return date, and vehicle plate number with someone who will call for help if you are late.
Keep at least an extra 2 gallons (7.6 L) of water per person sealed in the vehicle year-round.
If stuck in sand, letting tires down to about 20 PSI or less can help you drive out - carry a gauge and inflator to reinflate.
Sitting 1-2 feet off the ground on a cot, seat, or pile of brush is much cooler than sitting on hot sand.

sources.title: Heat and Cold Illness in Travelers (Yellow Book)

whenNotTo: Do not stay put if a flash flood, wildfire, or other immediate threat is coming at your location - move to safety first.
Do not start walking in daytime heat just because waiting feels hard; waiting in shade is usually the safer choice.

quickGlance.situation: You are stranded or lost in hot desert country with limited water.
immediate: Get into shade and stop all hard work in the heat
Stay with your vehicle and raise the hood
Drink when thirsty - save sweat, not water
Call or text 911 and try satellite SOS if your phone has it
then: Signal with a mirror by day and a light by night
If you must move, go at night along roads, and leave a note
Watch everyone for heat illness signs every hour

title: Hot, Humid, and Tropical Environments
summary: Humid heat stops sweat from cooling you, soaks your gear, and breeds insects and infection. This guide covers pacing, water, clothing, bugs, feet, and shelter in hot, wet country.

steps.title: Understand why humid heat is different
steps.body: Your body cools mostly by sweat evaporating off your skin. When the air is hot and humid - especially above about 95 F (35 C) - sweat drips off instead of evaporating, so you keep heating up even while soaked. That means you can get heat illness at temperatures that would feel manageable in dry country. Check the local heat forecast if you can (the CDC HeatRisk tool and the NWS heat index both factor in humidity). Treat a high heat index as a reason to slow down, not just a number. Wet clothing does not mean you are cooling well; a flushed, dizzy, or confused person is in trouble no matter how sweaty they are.

steps.title: Acclimatize and pace yourself
steps.body: Bodies adapt to heat, but slowly. Most of the change takes about 10 days of daily exercise in the heat, roughly 1-2 hours a day; just sitting in the heat gives only partial adaptation, and the benefit fades within days to weeks once you leave. In your first week, cut your workload and distance. Do hard work early in the morning and late in the afternoon, and rest in shade during midday. Take regular cooling breaks. Work in pairs and check each other. If anyone becomes faint or weak, stop all activity and get them cool. Heat exhaustion and heat stroke care are covered in the heat illness guides in the Medical category.

steps.title: Drink to thirst and replace salt
steps.body: Drink regularly and before you feel parched, but do not force huge amounts of plain water on someone who is not thirsty. Over-drinking plain water for hours can cause dangerously low blood sodium (hyponatremia), which can look like heat illness but with confusion and a normal body temperature. During long hot days - more than about 6 hours of work or heat exposure - eat salty food with your water or use oral rehydration salts (see medical-008). Avoid alcohol. Treat all jungle stream, swamp, and puddle water before drinking (see water-002 and water-008); tropical surface water often carries bacteria and parasites.

steps.title: Dress for sun, sweat, and bugs
steps.body: Wear loose, lightweight, light-colored clothing that lets air move. Long sleeves and long pants protect against sun, sharp leaves, leeches, and insects at the same time. A wide-brimmed hat cuts radiant heat. Synthetic or blended fabrics dry faster than heavy cotton. Mosquitoes are worst at dawn, at dusk, on overcast days, and in summer; in the tropics they can carry dengue, malaria, Zika, and other diseases. Use an EPA-registered insect repellent on exposed skin, following the label, and consider permethrin-treated clothing. Sleep under a mosquito net if one is available. For tick and mosquito control details, see medical-010.

steps.title: Protect your feet and skin
steps.body: Constant wet is the enemy. Feet that stay wet for days get immersion foot (trench foot): wrinkled, white, painful, and later blistered or infected skin. Every rest stop, take boots off, dry and air your feet, and change into dry socks if you have them; keep one dry pair just for sleeping. Small cuts and scrapes get infected fast in humid heat. Clean every wound promptly with safe water, cover it, and watch for spreading redness, warmth, pus, or fever. Keep skin folds dry to prevent rashes. Check yourself for ticks and leeches daily; pull leeches off from the head end or let them drop, and keep the bite clean.

steps.title: Sleep off the ground and stay dry
steps.body: The jungle floor is wet and full of ants, scorpions, snakes, and runoff when it rains. Sleep raised off the ground in a hammock or a raised platform with a tarp roof (see shelter-010). Pitch on slightly high ground, never in a gully or near a stream that can rise. Look up before you camp - dead branches and rotten trees fall without warning, especially in storms. Shake out boots, clothes, and bedding before use. Store food sealed and away from your sleeping spot to avoid drawing animals and insects. Expect heavy afternoon rain and lightning in many tropical areas; plan to be under cover by then.

steps.title: Travel carefully in dense vegetation
steps.body: Thick growth limits visibility to a few yards, so it is easy to get lost. Follow streams downhill or existing trails rather than cutting new routes, and mark your path. Move slowly, look where you put your hands and feet, and use a stick to part vegetation. Many tropical plants have spines or irritating sap - do not grab plants for balance without looking. Rivers in the tropics can rise fast after rain upstream; cross only when necessary and follow env-009. If you are lost, stopping and signaling usually beats pushing deeper into unknown terrain (see env-005).

warnings: High humidity hides heat stress - confusion, collapse, or strange behavior in the heat is an emergency even if the person is sweating.
Drinking large amounts of plain water for many hours without food or salt can cause dangerous low sodium.
Never drink untreated tropical surface water.
Feet left wet for days can develop immersion foot, which can lead to serious infection.
Do not camp under dead trees or in gullies that can flood.
proTips: Carry two pairs of socks and rotate them - wear one while the other dries on the outside of your pack.
A small packet of oral rehydration salts weighs almost nothing and is worth carrying in every hot-weather kit.
Plan your hardest effort for first light; tropical afternoons are often the hottest and stormiest part of the day.
Light-colored clothing makes ticks easier to see.

sources.title: Heat and Cold Illness in Travelers (Yellow Book)

whenNotTo: Do not push through the first week of heat exposure at full workload - acclimatization takes days.
Do not rely on this guide for treating heat stroke; use the Medical category and get help.

quickGlance.situation: You are working, traveling, or stranded in hot, humid, or jungle conditions.
immediate: Slow down and rest in shade during midday
Drink regularly and eat salty food on long days
Cover skin and use repellent against mosquitoes
then: Dry your feet and change socks at every stop
Sleep off the ground on high, safe ground
Treat all water before drinking

title: Cold and Arctic Environments - Wind Chill, Travel, and Staying Dry
summary: How cold, wind, and wet steal heat, how to read wind chill and the new NWS cold alerts, and how to use the COLD principle, layers, and smart travel to stay warm and dry.

steps.title: Know how cold takes your heat
steps.body: Your body loses heat fastest through contact with water or wet clothing (conduction), then through wind (convection), then by radiating it to cold surroundings. That is why wet and windy days at 35 F (2 C) can be more dangerous than calm, dry days far below zero. Sitting on snow or bare cold ground also pulls heat out quickly. Every decision in cold country comes back to three things: stay dry, block the wind, and insulate yourself from the ground. People who are tired, hungry, dehydrated, older, very young, or sick lose heat faster and need more protection.

steps.title: Read wind chill and cold alerts
steps.body: Wind chill is how cold it feels on exposed skin when wind strips heat away. The NWS index is designed for adults at face height, at night with no sun; bright sun can make it feel 10-18 F warmer. Example: at 0 F (-18 C) with a 15 mph wind, the wind chill is about -19 F (-28 C), and exposed skin can freeze in about 30 minutes. Frostbite needs the actual air temperature to be below freezing, but hypothermia can happen well above freezing. Since the 2024-25 winter, the NWS replaced its Wind Chill alerts: a Wind Chill Watch is now an Extreme Cold Watch, a Wind Chill Warning is now an Extreme Cold Warning, and a Wind Chill Advisory is now a Cold Weather Advisory. These new alerts can be issued for dangerous cold even without wind.

steps.title: Dress by the COLD principle
steps.body: The Army uses the acronym COLD for cold-weather clothing. C - keep it Clean: dirt and body oils crush insulation. O - avoid Overheating: sweat soaks your layers and then freezes you when you stop, so shed a layer before you start sweating. L - wear it Loose and in Layers: tight clothes cut blood flow, and layers trap warm air and let you adjust. D - keep it Dry: change wet socks and gloves right away and keep a dry set for sleeping. A good layer system is a moisture-wicking base layer, an insulating middle layer like fleece or wool, and a hooded windproof and waterproof shell. Cover your head, neck, hands, and feet well. Avoid cotton next to your skin.

steps.title: Fuel, hydrate, and check each other
steps.body: Your body burns more calories just to stay warm. Eat frequent snacks with fat and carbohydrates, and eat something before sleeping. Drink warm fluids if you can; cold air is dry and you lose a lot of water by breathing, but cold also dulls thirst. Pale yellow urine is a good sign. Pair up and check each other's faces, ears, nose, and fingers often for white, gray, waxy, or numb patches (frostnip and frostbite). Watch for shivering, stumbling, slurred speech, poor decisions, or 'the umbles' - those signal hypothermia. Care for frostbite and hypothermia is covered in the cold injury guides in the Medical category; the first move is always to get the person out of wind and wet and into insulation.

steps.title: Travel smart on snow and ice
steps.body: Travel during daylight and plan to stop with at least an hour of light left to make camp. Keep a steady pace that does not make you sweat. Short days, deep snow, and whiteouts make distances take two to three times longer than in summer. Snowshoes or skis keep you from post-holing, which wastes energy and soaks your legs. Stay off frozen lakes and rivers unless you have checked the ice (see env-010), and avoid steep, snow-loaded slopes (see env-011). In a whiteout, stop and shelter rather than wandering - it is easy to walk in circles or off a drop. If stranded in a vehicle, stay with it, run the engine only about 10 minutes an hour for heat, and keep the exhaust pipe clear of snow to avoid carbon monoxide (see medical-047).

steps.title: Shelter early and insulate from the ground
steps.body: Do not wait until you are exhausted or hypothermic to shelter. Get out of the wind first: behind trees, rocks, or a snow wall. Put as much insulation as you can under you - a pad, packs, spruce boughs, or dry brush - because the ground steals more heat than the air. Small shelters warm up faster than big ones. A snow shelter can be much warmer than the outside air if built well (see shelter-003), and shelter-008 covers getting through a cold night without a kit. If you can make fire safely, it dries gear and boosts morale (see fire-010). Melt snow for water instead of eating it, which chills you (see water-013).

steps.title: Protect hands, feet, and face
steps.body: Fingers, toes, ears, nose, and cheeks freeze first. Mittens are warmer than gloves; wear thin liner gloves underneath for tasks so you never handle metal or fuel bare-handed (super-cooled fuel can cause instant frostbite). Wiggle toes and fingers often, and loosen tight boots. Warm cold hands in your armpits or against a partner's belly. Do not rub frozen skin or warm it by a fire or engine you cannot feel - you can burn numb skin without knowing. If skin has frozen and there is a chance it could refreeze before you reach safety, it is usually better to keep it frozen than thaw and refreeze it; get medical care as soon as possible.

warnings: Sweating in the cold is dangerous - wet layers lose most of their insulation and chill you fast when you stop.
Hypothermia can happen at temperatures well above freezing, especially with rain, wind, or immersion.
Never run a stove, heater, or generator inside a closed tent, snow shelter, or vehicle without ventilation - carbon monoxide kills.
Do not rub frostbitten skin or rewarm it with direct high heat.
Alcohol makes you feel warm while increasing heat loss.
proTips: Open your jacket and take off your hat before climbing a hill; put them back on at the top before you cool down.
Sleep with tomorrow's socks, gloves, water bottle, and phone inside your sleeping bag to keep them dry and working.
Keep phone and spare batteries in an inner pocket - cold drains batteries fast.
A fresh dry pair of socks is worth more than an extra jacket on a long cold trip.
